title: Zechariah: not by might (Zechariah 4:6)
hookLine: read on Hanukkah: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit"

lines: A GOLDEN LAMPSTAND, TWO OLIVE TREES.
cards: The angel comes back and wakes him. In the King James, Zechariah is waked "as a man that is wakened out of his sleep." Groggy, he's asked what he sees.
A lampstand, all of gold, with a bowl on top and seven lamps. And beside it, one on each side, two olive trees.
Golden pipes run from the trees, so the oil flows straight to the light, and nobody has to carry a single jar. Zechariah asks the obvious thing: "What are these, my lord?"
And the answer doesn't sound like an answer at all.

teach.b: Instead of a key to the symbols, he's handed a message for someone else. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."
The message is for Zerubbabel, a leader of the people who came back from exile in Babylon. His job is rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem, and the chapter hints that the work looks too big.

teach.h: O GREAT MOUNTAIN, BECOME A PLAIN.
teach.b: So the next line names the problem: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain."
Whatever is piled in his way, rubble, opposition, a people too tired to begin, will be leveled, and not by an army.

teach.h: NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER, BUT BY MY SPIRIT.
teach.b: Then a promise in plain building terms: "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it."

teach.h: WHO HATH DESPISED THE DAY OF SMALL THINGS?
teach.b: And a question that is really a rebuke to the doubters: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" A foundation is small. A first stone is small.
The people looking at it were tempted to scoff. Now put the vision back together: a lamp fed straight from living trees, with no one straining to haul the oil.
Some readers hear that as the whole message in one picture: the light keeps burning, and it isn't muscle that keeps it lit.

teach.h: READ ON THE SHABBAT OF HANUKKAH.
teach.b: Jews read this passage in synagogue on the Shabbat of Hanukkah: a golden lamp, a holiday of lights, and, some hear, a reminder that what is celebrated was not, in the end, about might.

how: Jews read Zechariah's vision of the golden lampstand as the prophetic reading on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, and the line "not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit" is sung and quoted during the holiday.

o: the governor who laid the new Temple's foundation
the prophet who saw a gold lamp and heard: not by might
a king of Judah who melted down the Temple's gold lamp

games.q: not by might — tap the pairs.

s: "not by might" was first spoken to the Maccabees
in Zechariah it's a message to Zerubbabel, rebuilding the Temple. Jews read it on the Shabbat of Hanukkah.
in the vision, oil flows from olive trees straight to the lamp
golden pipes run from the trees, so no one has to carry the oil.
Zechariah is told the work is too small to matter
the opposite: "who hath despised the day of small things?"

games.q: you're Zerubbabel. the Temple is a foundation and a heap of rubble, and people scoff at how small it is. what are you told?
o: raise an army and force it through.
not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit.
give up and wait for a richer generation.
games.why: the mountain in his way will become a plain, and the hands that laid the foundation will finish it.

practice: Bring to mind one problem you've been trying to win by force, an argument you keep pushing, a person you keep pressing, and name your great mountain.

Then ask what the small first stone would be: not the whole solution, one gentle step, a question instead of a demand, a pause instead of a push, asking for help. If you pray, you can hold Zechariah's line for a while.

wordCard.voice: Zechariah. The prophet who saw a golden lamp fed by two olive trees, and carried a message to a weary builder. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: "not by might, nor by power," the opening of Zechariah 4:6.

carryVoice: Your line: not by might. The day of small things counts too. Day eight hundred thirty, done.
